extracted.intended_audience: aspiring authors, essayists, and general readers interested in literary conduct and style
extracted.subtask_description: Prescriptive and critical guidance for would-be authors and essayists on qualifications, tone, use of familiar tropes, character-keeping, and how to treat disagreement and moral subjects in prose. Covers both practical writerly standards and thematic/philosophical guidance for content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Keeping of character in correspondence
rubrics_metrics.description: Johnson was too apt to destroy the keeping of character in his correspondences. A retired trader might desire a little more slumber, 'a little folding of the hands to sleep;' but the lofty malignity of a fallen spirit sickening at the beams of day, would not be among the feelings of an ordinary mind.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain a consistent and believable voice for each character or persona in letters and narrative. Avoid attributing extravagant, elevated, or incongruous feelings or diction to commonplace people; preserve plausibility of character. (Example given: do not ascribe the lofty malignity of a 'fallen spirit' to a retired trader.) See Miss Talbot's Letters to Mrs. Carter for examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acknowledge limited perspective on complex questions
rubrics_metrics.description: In questions diffuse and compounded... disagreement of opinion will always be multiplied; not because we are irrational, but because we are finite beings, furnished with different kinds of knowledge, exerting different degrees of attention, one discovering consequences which escape another...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When treating complicated or multi‑faceted subjects, accept and signal that reasonable people may disagree. Writers should show awareness of the partiality of their own view, avoid claiming universal verdicts, and explicitly consider different kinds of evidence, purposes, and criteria that lead others to other conclusions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moderation and forbearance in tone toward dissent
rubrics_metrics.description: This inconstancy and unsteadiness... ought certainly to teach us moderation and forbearance towards those who cannot accommodate themselves to our sentiments: if they are deceived, we have no right to attribute their mistake to obstinacy or negligence...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adopt a charitable, tolerant tone in polemic and critical writing. Avoid personal attacks and attributing bad faith to opponents; acknowledge one's own capacity for error and the possibility of future change in belief. This fosters persuasive, civil discourse.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of perennial poetic topicks (familiar imagery is effective)
rubrics_metrics.description: There are certain topicks which never are exhausted... When a poet mentions the spring, we know that the zephyrs are about to whisper... yet who is there so insensible of the beauties of nature... as not to feel his heart bound at the mention of the spring?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not dismiss conventional images or motifs as worthless; familiar tropes (spring, night, groves, limpid brooks) retain emotive power and may be used effectively. Familiarity is not necessarily banality: conventional scenes can still move readers if well rendered.

rubrics_metrics.name: Urgency of the present (carpe diem theme as moral/writerly prompt)
rubrics_metrics.description: The precept that directs us to use the present hour, and refer nothing to a distant time... every moralist may venture to inculcate, because it will always be approved, and because it is always forgotten.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When arguing for moral improvement or action in essays and rhetoric, emphasize immediacy and the risk of delay. Use concrete exempla (e.g., sudden death, lives cut short) to persuade readers that postponement undermines good intentions; exhortation should stress present opportunity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authors must have proper qualifications and useful matter
rubrics_metrics.description: Let it be deeply impressed... that he who has not obtained the proper qualifications of an author, can have no excuse for the arrogance of writing, but the power of imparting to mankind something necessary to be known.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Justify publication on the basis of knowledge or utility: writers should possess sufficient understanding or experience to speak authoritatively, and their work should aim to impart something necessary or beneficial. Avoid writing from mere vanity; authority and usefulness legitimize authorship.

rubrics_metrics.name: Portrayal of labour and struggle as valuable subject and condition
rubrics_metrics.description: To strive with difficulties, and to conquer them, is the highest human felicity; the next is, to strive, and deserve to conquer... labour, though unsuccessful, is more eligible than idleness; he that prosecutes a lawful purpose by lawful means, acts always with the approbation of his own reason.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Favor themes and narratives that depict effort, perseverance, and moral striving. In both theme choice and characterization, present labour and the pursuit of worthy ends as sources of dignity and fulfillment rather than mere background; this lends ethical weight and reader sympathy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Critique comparative desires and counterfeit advantages
rubrics_metrics.description: Many of our miseries are merely comparative: we are often made unhappy, not by the presence of any real evil, but by the absence of some fictitious good... an impartial inquiry into the real worth of that which is so ardently desired.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When treating social status, wealth, or inherited honours, interrogate whether the objects of desire have intrinsic worth. Use essays to expose 'counterfeit advantages'—things coveted through comparison—and to prompt readers to weigh real goods versus imagined ones; deploy irony and example to deflate vanity.
